d.title: Thirty-one method names, in four groups
d.caption: **You have already met most of the ones that matter**, and the groups are what the list is for. The three server-to-client requests are lesson 1.4's subject. The `notifications/*` family is fire-and-forget with no reply. **And `tasks/*` is a newer surface for work that outlives a request** — treat it as optional and check the capability rather than assuming, exactly as for sampling.

d.title: Two error layers, and the one most people conflate
d.caption: **A JSON-RPC error means the request failed; an `isError` result means the request succeeded and the tool did not.** That is why lesson 2.3's measurement showed an unknown tool coming back as a *result* rather than as `METHOD_NOT_FOUND` — `tools/call` was a perfectly valid method call, and the tool inside it was the problem. **Keeping them apart matters when reading a trace:** a −32601 is a client bug or a version mismatch, and an `isError` is a conversation about the tool.

items.label: -32600 INVALID_REQUEST / -32601 METHOD_NOT_FOUND
items.sub: a client bug, or a revision mismatch

items.label: -32000 CONNECTION_CLOSED, -32042 URL_ELICITATION_REQUIRED
items.sub: MCP's own two, outside the band

items.label: a result with isError: True
items.sub: the call worked; the tool did not

d.title: Three requests, and what the server is borrowing
d.caption: **A server holds no model, has no user and sees no filesystem beyond its own**, and each of these asks the client for exactly one of those. The rationale is the same throughout: the host already has the model, the user and the file access, so the server asks rather than acquiring its own API key, prompt surface or paths. **Which is a good design, and also why these are the three most consequential capabilities in the protocol** — section 05.

d.title: The server's end: ctx.session, and ctx.elicit
d.caption: **`ctx.elicit` takes a Pydantic schema**, so the user's answer arrives typed rather than as free text — the same contract idea as lesson 2.2's output schemas, pointed at a person instead of a model. Sampling and roots go through `ctx.session`, which is the server's end of the connection. **Note what the tool returns when the user says no:** the schema's own fields carry the answer, so the tool branches on `proceed` rather than on the request having completed.

nodes.sub: a Pydantic model, so the answer is typed

nodes.label: Then branch on proceed
nodes.sub: which is what they actually said

d.title: Passing the callback is what declares the capability
d.caption: **There is no separate flag to set** — the client supplies a function and the capability is declared for it. Each callback is the host's decision rather than the server's, which is the whole design: the server asks and the host answers however it chooses. **And read the elicitation result carefully:** `action=accept` means the user engaged with the dialogue, while `proceed: false` is their answer, so a server checking only `action` has read a refusal as consent.

d.title: No callbacks: three failed calls, not three degraded ones
d.caption: **Not a reduced result — a failed call.** The tool raised, the error reached the caller as `isError: True`, and the message names the missing capability. So a server built on any of these three does not work at all for a host that has not implemented them, which is the fact that decides whether you can use them. **Tools and resources work everywhere; these work where the host chose to support them**, and host support is much thinner here than for anything in lesson 1.3.

d.title: What each one hands over
d.caption: **Granting sampling is materially like handing over an API key:** the server chooses the prompt, it runs on your model, and it is billed to you — which also runs lesson 4.1's injection problem in both directions, since your model reads text the server composed and the result returns to the server. **Elicitation is the one that borrows your credibility:** the message is the server's text rendered by your interface, so *“enter your API key to continue”* is a phishing prompt with your branding around it.

state: servers you would give a key

d.title: Six RFCs, and why you should not implement an authorisation server
d.caption: **An MCP server is an OAuth 2.1 resource server: it validates tokens and does not issue them.** Point `issuer_url` at the identity provider your organisation already runs, implement `TokenVerifier` against its public keys, set `resource_server_url` so the audience check has something to compare — and every hard part stays with the provider. **Note the last row:** resource indicators are what make the audience check meaningful, so skipping that check discards most of what these RFCs buy you.

d.title: A registry is discovery, not review
d.caption: **A listing says a server exists and is described — not that anyone reviewed what its tools do or what credentials it holds.** And the rug pull from lesson 4.1 gets *easier* with a registry rather than harder, because the install is one line and the version is often implicit. **So a registry raises the value of the two controls that notice a server changing after you looked at it:** a pinned version, and a hash of the tool list. Treat it the way you treat a package index.
